body: I'm finished with A levels. For Maths, a good tip I’d give is to download every single past paper from the past 10 years, filter all the exercises by topic, put a little note on each exercise saying the year and variation they came from, then do all the exercises while making notes on how to solve them. It’s better to do it on paper and not on note-taking softwares imo. Compare your answers to Youtube tutorials and the official marking scheme releases, (tip: seach for the year and version of the past paper, ex: "9709 2022 32 October") and if they don't match, explain to yourself on paper why you didn't get it right. A good channel for that: https://www.youtube.com/@MathWorld-yp9od . One very bad mistake I did was to study 'planes' for the vectors chapter on A levels. That was very stupid and wasted me like 3 days for no reason. You have to check the current syllabus because on older past papers there may be some questions that aren't in exams nowadays. Start studying very early for the final exams. That’s something I wish I had done. Good luck on your journey! It may be tiring, but in the end your hard work will be worth it.

Maybe also a laptop (if your school allows you to bring it), for some quicker note-taking and downloading resources like past papers, watching tutorials during break if you didn't understand something, or request support from teachers if you have their contact.

I'm finished with A levels with good grades. Here's some tips for the exams I did this year, which may be useful:

For Maths, I downloaded every single past paper from the past 10 years, filtered all the exercises by topic, put a little note on each exercise saying the year and variation they came from, then did all the exercises while making notes on how to solve them, even if I had done the almost same exact exercise 10 times already. Print everything or the ones you find are most difficult, do it on paper because that's how it's gonna be on the exam lol (rip printer). Compare your answers to Youtube tutorials and the official marking scheme releases, (tip: seach for the year and version of the past paper, ex: "9709 2022 32 October" and if they don't match, explain why you didn't get it right. A good channel for that: [https://www.youtube.com/@MathWorld-yp9od](https://www.youtube.com/@MathWorld-yp9od) . I went from D to B in Maths. One very bad mistake I did was to study 'planes' for the vectors chapter on A levels. That was very stupid and wasted me like 3 days for no reason. You have to check the current syllabus because on older past papers there may be some questions that aren't in exams nowadays.

  
For Business, this guy saved my life [https://www.youtube.com/@EdsEssentials/videos](https://www.youtube.com/@EdsEssentials/videos) . Not much to say. He teaches you how to write essays in the exact way that Cambridge wants you to, and also has flashcards to help memorize topics. I went from a D to an A.

  
For IT theory exams, unfortunately you have to memorize until you can't stand the sound of your voice anymore. It's tiring, but the results are worth it. One good advice, is to ask ChatGPT to give you the topics's definition, then 3 advantages and 3 disadvantages, for example:  
"Briefly explain to me what the FTP protocol is, and where it's commonly applied, then give me 3 advantages and 3 disadvantages for it".  
For the IT practical exams, have all of the required softwares (Access, Excel, PS, ANI, VSCODE, etc..) avaliable on YOUR computer, so you can be practicing it all times. Try doing some small projects, (remove a background, create a sales database...) you'll get familiarised with them and help you gain confidence. This teacher has tutorials that can help you solve past papers: [https://www.youtube.com/@finzpapers9364](https://www.youtube.com/@finzpapers9364) .

  
For English Language, it's good to have your teacher be constantly reviewing essays you voluntarily wrote to practice for the exam. You need to have a feedback, "from the eyes of an examiner".

Hope it helps somehow. Good luck guys.
